blocks.text: 1. Supervised Learning

blocks.alt: Input feeds a model that produces a known output

blocks.text: Types of Machine Learning, the previous topic, previewed Supervised Learning first among the four major types. Supervised Learning means every single training example comes paired with its correct, already-known answer, unlike the other types covered elsewhere in this module.

The model's job is to learn the mapping connecting each input to its correct answer, well enough that it can generalize that learned mapping to genuinely new inputs it has never actually seen before. This makes Supervised Learning the most common, most direct starting point for a real Machine Learning project, whenever the necessary labeled data is actually available.
2. Input-Output Pairs

blocks.alt: Each input is paired with its own matching output

blocks.text: A Supervised Learning dataset is made up of input-output pairs. The input consists of the features describing one particular example, a house's size, location, and age for instance, exactly the kind of features already introduced in the What Is Machine Learning topic.

The output is the correct, already-known answer for that same example, that same house's actual, real sale price in this example. The model's entire job is learning the relationship connecting these inputs to these outputs, a relationship it can then apply to a brand new input where the correct output is not yet actually known.
3. Two Genuinely Distinct Flavors

blocks.alt: Supervised learning splits into classification and regression

blocks.text: Supervised Learning splits into two genuinely distinct flavors, depending on what kind of answer is actually being predicted. Regression applies when the correct answer is a number, predicting a house's price, a temperature, or a stock's value, all covered in depth in their own dedicated module later in this course.

Classification applies when the correct answer is instead a category, predicting whether an email is spam or not spam, or whether a patient has a disease or does not, covered in equal depth in the Classification Algorithms module later on. Recognizing which flavor a given problem actually calls for is one of the very first practical decisions in any Supervised Learning project.

blocks.text: 4. The Training Process

blocks.alt: The model predicts, compares to the real answer, adjusts, and repeats

blocks.text: The training process itself follows a simple, repeated loop. The model makes a guess for a given training example, that guess then gets compared directly against the actual, already-known correct answer for that example, and the size of the resulting error gets measured.

The model then gets adjusted slightly to reduce that measured error, and this entire loop repeats across the training data, gradually shaping the model toward making increasingly accurate guesses over time. This loop, guess, compare, measure error, adjust, is the core mechanism underlying essentially every Supervised Learning algorithm covered later in this course.
5. The Real Goal Is Generalization

blocks.alt: A model fits training data well, but the real test is new, unseen data

blocks.text: The real goal of Supervised Learning is not simply memorizing the specific training examples it was shown, but genuinely learning the underlying pattern connecting inputs to outputs. A model that only memorizes its training examples performs poorly on new, unseen data, a problem called overfitting, covered in far more depth later in this course.

A model that genuinely learns the underlying pattern, rather than merely memorizing specific examples, performs well on new examples it has never actually encountered before, exactly the property that makes a Supervised Learning model genuinely useful once deployed in the real world.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A model that achieves near-perfect accuracy on its own training data is not automatically a good sign. It can just as easily mean the model has memorized those specific examples rather than genuinely learning a pattern that generalizes.

blocks.text: 6. Familiar, Real-World Examples

Supervised Learning already shows up in familiar, everyday systems. Email spam filtering, trained on a large collection of emails already labeled spam or not spam by real people, is a classic, clear Classification example, directly echoing the spam example already introduced in the What Is Machine Learning topic.

Predicting a house's likely sale price from a history of past sales where the actual sale price is already known is a classic Regression example instead, the exact same house-price scenario already used to illustrate the core recipe in that same earlier topic.
7. A Genuine Requirement: Labeled Data

blocks.alt: Raw data becomes ready for training only after a human labels it

blocks.text: A genuine requirement Supervised Learning simply cannot avoid is that every single training example needs its correct answer already attached before training can even begin. Labeling data by hand, or collecting it from some process that naturally produces labels as a byproduct, is very often the hardest, most genuinely expensive part of an entire Supervised Learning project.

This exact constraint, the real cost and effort of obtaining labeled data, is precisely what motivates Semi-Supervised Learning, covered later in this module, an approach specifically designed for situations where fully labeling an entire dataset simply is not practical.
8. Algorithms Covered Later in This Course

This course covers many specific Supervised Learning algorithms in genuine depth in later modules. Linear and Logistic Regression, covered in their own dedicated modules, are among the most foundational, widely used starting points.

Decision Trees, Random Forests, and other Classification algorithms follow, along with Support Vector Machines, K-Nearest Neighbors, and several others, each covered with its own worked examples, tradeoffs, and appropriate use cases in the modules specifically dedicated to them.

blocks.text: 9. When Supervised Learning Is Genuinely the Right Fit

blocks.alt: Having labeled examples points to supervised learning as a good fit

blocks.text: Supervised Learning is genuinely the right fit whenever clear, correct historical examples already exist, the single strongest signal that a Supervised Learning approach will actually work well for a given problem.

It also fits whenever the actual goal is predicting one specific, well-defined answer, a price, a category, a yes-or-no outcome, rather than discovering some unknown structure the data might contain, the genuinely different goal that instead calls for Unsupervised Learning, covered in the very next topic.
10. Worked Example
The example below trains a simple Supervised Learning classifier on labeled examples, then uses it to predict the correct category for a new, unseen example.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# Each row: [hours studied, practice tests taken]; label: 1 = passed exam, 0 = did not pass
X = np.array([[1, 0], [5, 2], [2, 1], [8, 4], [3, 1], [7, 3]])
y = np.array([0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1])  # the correct, known answer for every training example

model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=42)
model.fit(X, y)  # training: guess, compare to known answer, adjust, repeat

new_student = np.array([[6, 2]])
prediction = model.predict(new_student)

print(f"Training accuracy: {model.score(X, y):.2f}")
print(f"Prediction for a new student (6 hours studied, 2 practice tests): {'passed' if prediction[0] == 1 else 'did not pass'}")
print("\nThe model learned this mapping entirely from the labeled input-output pairs it was given")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Every single training example here included its correct answer, whether that student actually passed, exactly the defining requirement of Supervised Learning covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Supervised Learning trains on input-output pairs where the correct answer is already known for every example.
The model learns the mapping from inputs to correct outputs, generalizing it to new, unseen inputs.
Regression predicts a number; Classification predicts a category, the two genuinely distinct flavors.
Training repeats a loop: guess, compare to the known answer, measure error, and adjust.
The real goal is generalization, learning the underlying pattern, not memorizing the training examples.
Spam filtering and house price prediction are classic, familiar Classification and Regression examples.
Every training example needs its correct answer already attached, often the hardest, most expensive part.
This course covers many Supervised Learning algorithms in depth later, including Regression, Decision Trees, and more.
Next up: Unsupervised Learning, covering how a system finds structure with no correct answers provided at all.
